utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, Madam Registrar and Happy New Year.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Happy New Year to you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you call the case now, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Brdjanin. Can you follow the proceedings in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I can hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. And good morning. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, Anna Richterova, Julian Nicholls and Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to the three of you. Appearances for Radoslav Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I'm attorney Milan Trbojevic, assisted by co-counsel [as interpreted] John Ackerman and our assistants Marela Jevtovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to the three of you. Let's bring in the witness. The interpretation says assisted. You have promoted yourself, Mr. Trbojevic. And Mr. Ackerman has become co-counsel. So that's all --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's mistake, sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Now you don't have any reason to grumble, Mr. Brdjanin. Yes, Madam Richterova?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We have some preliminaries which we would like to solve before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With regard to this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is with respect to the next witness. It is rather important that technical things are solved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see. I am anticipating what we are in for. Yes, tell me. Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I actually have two matters, Your Honour, if we could go into closed session for the first one or private session, rather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, we go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session. So let's bring the witness in, please. How long do you anticipate your cross to last, Mr. Trbojevic? I know but we have got very few questions left on the part of the Prosecution. This is so that we can --

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that I will be through within an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment because I had it on number 0. One hour? Okay. Thank you. So we should have the break as soon as we finish with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Alic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, you have not finished. May I ask you to make the solemn declaration once more before you continue and finish your testimony, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Alic. You may sit down. Madam Richterova will be finishing her examination-in-chief her direct, and then you will be cross-examined by the Defence. Madam Richterova, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Alic. I have only a couple of additional questions. And the first is yesterday you mentioned that there were checkpoints in the vicinity of Bosanski Novi town and that these checkpoints moved from time to time. Do you know who manned these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And second question is: You said that Branko Balaban called all three men, Samid Imsirevic, Camil Alic, and Fehim Mehmedagic and that he shot them dead. And after that, a military vehicle came by, stopped, and there was this officer who told you that you should go towards the Japra compound. How soon after this incident, this officer arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps five minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Could this officer see what happened?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He couldn't have, because it happened before his arrival, but he could have seen the dead men lying on the road, and the other people who emerged from the other road, from the direction of Sikare, the hamlet of Sikare.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: With respect to this officer, do you remember whether he wore any insignia?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he wore insignia, but at that moment, I was seized by fear. I wasn't really looking. I wasn't interested.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also said that you knew almost every -- all these soldiers who were present in Blagaj Japra. Where did you know them from?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were mainly my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your neighbours, do you know from which villages?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know. Maslovare, Svodna, Josava. These three villages mainly. Also the village of Petkovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what was their ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And do you remember whether they all wore uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. All of them were in uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And apart from the officer you mentioned, that he arrived in that jeep, did you notice anyone who could be in charge of these people in Blagaj Japra, when you were gathered and -- when you were gathered in Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I think it was -- let me remember his name. His last name was Popovic and his nickname was Pop. I can't remember his first name. It eludes me at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to show you one document, if I may ask the usher to show the witness P1628. As I said, we do not have translation of this document. Can we place it on the ELMO? Maybe it will be easier for the witness to read it, because I would like to obtain some translation through this witness. Mr. Alic, if maybe on the screen, it would be easier for you to read it, just tell us what is easier for you.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's more readable from the screen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you -- this is document dated 13 of October, 1999. Can you read the title of this document? Can you read it for us?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Record of exhumation, autopsies, and identification of dead bodies found in mass and individual graves in various localities in the area of Bosanski Novi municipality."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can we now go to the page 4? Can you put it a little bit lower? I would -- yeah. And more. Like this. Thank you. Can you read the first two lines for us, starting "dana"?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "On the 29th of September, 1999, at the locality of Blagaj Japra, "mezarje."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, Bosnian term for cemetery.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Coordinates, SK 150/874, located in the immediate vicinity of the elementary school on" -- you mean only the first two lines?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yeah, enough, thank you. And below, you will see listed names of people who were exhumed in that location, and it will be probably easier if I -- I will just read the name, and tell us whether you remember these people being with you in Blagaj Japra and what happened that person. You can see body number 1, Arapovic, Saban.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know the man. He was my neighbour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see him on 9 of June in Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see him on that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Begic, Hamdija.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hamdija Begic? I don't know the man at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Camil Alic?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my step brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see him in Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know what happened to him?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw him being killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Selimagic, Ismet?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you see him in Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were together in my father's house and we were driven out of my father's house together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What happened to him? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed, together with my brother, Alic, Camil, before my very eyes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mehmedagic, Fehim?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know him too. He was killed together with Alic, Camil.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Imsirevic Samid?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's my next door neighbour. He was killed together with Mehmedagic, Fehim, and Camil, Alic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Alic, Kemal?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my brother.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What happened to him?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was killed together with Ismet Selimagic, in the same spot.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And Selmic, Dervis?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him but I didn't see when he was killed. I heard he was killed but I didn't see it myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alic. This completed my examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Richterova. Sir, you are going to be cross-examined now, by Mr. Trbojevic, who is co-counsel together with Mr. John Ackerman in the Defence of the accused, Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin. I would like to give you a very important piece of advice before you start answering the questions that will be put to you on cross-examination. And that is that the lawyer, Mr. Trbojevic, who will be cross-examining you, is doing his duty here. He has a responsibility to look after the interests of his client and to defend his client in a court of justice where his client enjoys the presumption of innocence until he is proven guilty, if he is. So your responsibility, in turn, is a reciprocal one, in the sense that you are bound by law to answer each and every question that is put to you by him as truthfully and as fully as possible. You have no right to make a distinction between questions coming from the Prosecution and questions coming from the Defence. Your duty is to answer every question irrespective of who is putting it to you, as fully and truthfully as I have already explained to you. You will not answer any question if we tell you not to answer it. So Mr. Trbojevic, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examined by Mr. Trbojevic:

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Alic, I'll try and go through your testimony on the basis of a couple of questions so that we can get a couple of more data and maybe some explanations. In your statement that you made on the 1st of March of the year 2000, you said that a neighbour of yours, who was a police officer, said that new Serb uniforms for the police arrived, as well, and you gave the description of the insignia there. Could you tell us whether it was you yourself personally who saw those new Serb uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You did not see them about?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you did not see that new insignia?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were referring to the situation in Novi, about many vehicles and a lot of soldiers passing through on the way to Croatia. When it comes to the relationships between people in Novi, was it influenced in any way by the situation in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You could feel the winds of the war. People were frightened. You could see people holding up three fingers and shouting slogans and so people were frightened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Tell me whether you knew about the events happening in Gospic in October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know. I wasn't interested in any of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You did not hear about the fighting in the area of Gospic, about all the victims?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had not heard. I did hear that there was a war going on, but nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Trbojevic. Mr. Alic, when Mr. Trbojevic finishes with his question, please allow a little, small interval of time. The reason is a very simple one. You both speak the same language but we don't speak your language. So we need to receive interpretation. There are interpreters in the booths who are listening to what you are saying and then translating to us into English. So please, an interval of time is needed because otherwise if you jump straight away into answering the question without even letting Mr. Trbojevic finish his question, you will be causing us problems, all right? Okay. So let's give it a try. Mr. Trbojevic, next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you did not hear of the battles going on around Gospic?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I had not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you do know where Gospic is?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately, but I've never been there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you agree that Gospic is relatively close to Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all that close.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you ever have the opportunity to hear that quite a few refugees from Gospic area came to the area of Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you notice any Serb refugees from Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What are you referring to? 1992 or the end of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It is about the end of 1991 and the spring of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you're saying there were no Serb refugees from Croatia in Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in my building.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Trbojevic, he's not saying that there were no Serb refugees. He's saying that he doesn't know about the problem that you are mentioning. Doesn't mean to say that it did not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you hear about the events in the area of Kupres in the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you hear that the Croat units were fighting the Serbs in the Kupres area?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: According to your information, what do you know? What was happening in Kupres?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what was happening in other parts of the country. I can only tell you what was happening in my place of residence and its immediate surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that a certain number of refugees from Kupres had arrived to Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was living in Blagaj. They might have been there but I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were aware of the fact that quite a few representatives or members of the Serb forces, or rather the Yugoslav army at that time, before they left for Croatia and when they came back from the battle fields of Croatia represented a factor which caused some anxiety and concern among the citizens?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell me whether there were any reservists or demobilised soldiers from the Croat armed forces appearing in Novi or in the area?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I've never heard or seen anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: A short while ago, you mentioned that the reservists passing through used to shoot and that they created anxiety because they made these three-finger gestures?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Could you explain to us why this caused anxiety to the population?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Before the war I had never been interested in that, but I heard it from the elderly that it was a traditional Serb greeting to spite other people and whenever they saw a mosque, they would immediately start firing in the air and start swearing and all that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm asking you about this because on page 3 of your statement, you mention that somebody threatened the Muslims to cut off their two fingers so that they could greet people with three fingers as the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were threats of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Could you tell us who issued them?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uniformed people, I don't know who exactly. I didn't know them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you mean some of the uniformed people passing through Novi or some of your local uniformed people?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ones who were simply passing through.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned in your first statement, in your -- on page 2, paragraph 7, that from the village of Blagaj Japra, together with the Serbs from Svodna, you convened a meeting and you agreed that nothing bad would happen to anyone. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was Vitezovac not Svodna. Svodna is on the other side of the river, on the other bank. And this other village is on this side. So Svodna is on the left bank. It is a neighbouring village that I was talking about, the neighbouring village to Blagaj Japra.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. As you wish. It's not of essential importance to me. You said this neighbouring village is Svodna and we convened a meeting in our village and agreed with our neighbours and so on and so forth. However, it doesn't matter what village in particular it was. What matters to me is for to you tell me who agreed with whom.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present there in person. I know that some people of Muslim and some people of Serb nationality were there but I myself was not present.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know who was representing the Serbs and who was representing the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that there was Izet -- the President of SDA in Blagaj Japra, Izet Mehmedagic. I think he was there heading the delegation, and I don't know about anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know who was leading these negotiations on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you know what the topic of their talks was?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I can imagine, I wasn't present there, but probably the point was to make sure that nobody would come to any harm, that people would not be hurt or insulted or to prevent incidents of any sort. I suppose that was the point.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell me, when it comes to these talks between the two villages, was there anyone from the municipality there?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't suppose there was anyone there at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know if any of them went to the municipality to consult with anyone in relation to these talks?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean on the side of the Muslims or --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that when they -- when the refugees were driven out of the valley, I think Sifet went on that same evening, and I don't know about anyone else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In the same passage, you mentioned that you were listening to the radio and that you heard Serb nationalist songs?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And that people were continuing to say what happened to the Croats will happen to the Muslims as well?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was my personal assumption as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What nationalist songs do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nationalist songs, I can't remember exactly what the most popular ones were, but we perceived them as nationalist songs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Those were national Serb songs and --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is quoting Serb songs.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Who says that Serbia is a small country, is telling lies," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is there anything threatening for the Muslims in those songs?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there was nothing threatening. It was just a bit, well, you know. And then another quote, "One stone next to the other, Serbs next to one another, closing ranks," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When I asked you about this question, when you heard it said on the radio what happened to the Croats happened to the Muslims as well, you said it was your assumption?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Could you tell me exactly what you heard on the radio and what was your personal assumption? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My personal assumption was that we would meet the same fate because there were these calls from the Crisis Staff at the municipality of Bosanski Novi and there was this Ismet Selimagic who was secretary there, and he had to invite the Muslims to join in the war against Croatia, and he did issue an invitation but he was telling people, don't go, and that's why I assume that we would meet the same fate as they did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alic and Mr. Trbojevic, now, I would like to draw the attention of both of you, I have complaints, you're moving too fast, both of you, and you're not allowing a short interval of time between question and answer, and that's making the lives of the interpreters very difficult, with the result that we find it difficult to follow too. So please, for the umpteenth time, try to allow a short interval of time and go slower. Particularly you, Mr. Alic, you have a tendency it speak very fast. Reduce your speed a little bit because the interpreters need to follow better. Thanks. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was told that there was a slight mistake in the transcript so I'm going to turn to the witness and ask him to re-explain the situation once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Who was invited to do what and who was meant to distribute these invitations to citizens to be mobilised.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you to repeat what you answered.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean who was calling up the Muslims? I don't know who it was. I believe it was the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Bosanski Novi or maybe somebody else. I don't know who it could have been. The municipality of Bosanski Novi sent out these calls to Ismet Selimagic. He was told to distribute these invitations to the Muslims, and they were called up as reservists and they were called up to join in the war against Croatia, and the Muslims rejected it, and that's why I assumed that we would meet with the same fate as the Croats in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I would now like to ask you to tell us what you thought would happen to you?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that what would happen was what actually happened. That all assistance would be denied to us, that -- well, people were already beginning to be dismissed from their jobs. People of Muslim nationality, that is. And they were unable to buy groceries in the same way as the Serbs. They didn't enjoy the same rights as the Serbs did. And you could see the slogans, the graffiti everywhere, about Serbia and there were posters of Slobodan Milosevic in public buildings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We were discussing something else. You said that you assumed that the Muslims -- that the same thing would happen to the Muslims as happened to the Croats, and I'm asking you to explain to me what actually happened to the Croats, because in Croatia, the JNA did not stop the supplies for the Croats. It was actually the other way around. Of course, there was a conflict. I'm not going to argue about that, but this is why I'm asking you to explain to the Court what exactly was happening in Croatia that you feared would happen in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What happened in Croatia was this: Croatia was an internationally recognised state and the Serbs attacked it and they occupied as much as half of its territory and I was assuming that Bosnia and Herzegovina would probably be attacked in the same way because Bosnia and Herzegovina was a sovereign state in the same way as Croatia. I assumed that the same sort of war would break out there as happened in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you mentioned that it was impossible for the Muslims to buy groceries, to get medicines or fuel, as the other citizens of Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I myself, I had a shop of my own and I couldn't get fuel to restock my supplies. And if there was anyone sick in my family or my neighbours or anything, yes, I would go to the doctor and would get the prescription but when we went to get the medicines from the pharmacy, we would get the reply, no, no, no, we have nothing for you. Go to the Crisis Staff, ask for an extra certificate from them and then you will get the medicines.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Isn't it correct that most medicines would be bought for money at pharmacies?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, some people, even if they were willing to pay, could still not get the medicines.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can you tell us whether anybody had decided for the Muslims not to be entitled to supplies, food, fuel, et cetera, as opposed to the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You believe that there was a decision of this sort?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. And, well, I suppose the people working at the pharmacy, it didn't make any difference to them. It was all the same to them whether they were selling their medicines to the Muslims or the Serbs. It was all the same from their point of view, but probably they were not allowed and so that's why they said no.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You talked about the curfew. Do you know why a curfew was imposed?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us how long it lasted? I didn't quite understand what you said when you first mentioned it.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a certain period of time during the day when we were free to move about, go out and get the firewood or feed the animals -- well, that's all that we were allowed to do since we were living in the country but we could do nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was it put somewhere in writing?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they said it on the radio, and it was always emphasised that we had to respect that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How was it controlled?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I never went anywhere. What food I had, we could eat, and I never went anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there any patrols going through the villages and checking it?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There must have been. I wasn't living on the main road. I was a bit further away in the hamlet of Sikare. Yes, I suppose there must have been. The people who could have seen it were the ones living along the main road. That was the main road going through the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can you tell me whether there were any patrols of the citizens of Muslim nationality in the villages with mostly Muslim population, for any security checks or patrols?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. All the weapons had already been taken away from the Muslims, and that applies even to the ones who were reserve policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm referring to the spring of 1992. That was the time when these shortages were happening and these talks were taking place.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know what you're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there any patrols in the Muslim villages, any Muslim patrols, in order to prevent any incidents, banditry or what have you?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that as of January, maybe up until March or April, there were joint units, police reservists. There was a checkpoint at the Blagaj Japra bridge and there were two, three, four people together. And there were Serbs as well. And then afterwards, when things changed, Muslims relinquished their arms and the Serbs remained.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you agree -- do you agree with me that there were overall food shortages in town? And the same applied for fuel?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree. Because I myself, I had my own shop in Blagaj Japra, and I was unable to get supplies from the warehouses.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Tell me, did you know that in the organisation of Merhamet, the humanitarian organisation, there was something like a pharmacy?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew about that but I didn't visit it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: On page 3, you said that on Saturday, the 9th of May, weapons were gathered and turned over. Somebody drove them to the point of turning over?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Izet Mehmedagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said it was taken to members of the civilian Defence. Did you really mean the civilian defence?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who it was who took -- who he took the weapons to. He took them to the building of the municipality. He was told to go to the municipality. I don't know who it was before the municipality, who is supposed to take the weapons over. I wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Why was it taken by truck, if it was an insignificant quantity?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This Izet person, he owned a small shop as well, and he was with his pickup in front of the school building. And when we were deciding who would take the weapons, he said, "I will," and he put the weapons on his pickup and drove them away. It wasn't really in the trailer. He put all the weapons in the cabin of the truck, in the cab.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And he returned the same weapons the same day?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The story was that they only laughed at him and told him, "We don't need that. Take it away."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And then you testified about an event where a vehicle of the military police was attacked?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Some place between Blagaj Japra and Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Djurim is the place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said the attack was orchestrated, staged?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you an eyewitness?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't. I wasn't an eyewitness but that vehicle left in perfect working order. Nobody was hurt. And that's why we are assuming - not only I but all of my fellow townsfolk - that it was staged because immediately after that attack, the shelling of Blagaj began. We suppose that the only purpose of that so-called attack was to provide an excuse for the shelling of Blagaj. I believe they had no other way of starting the shelling.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So it's logical deduction on your part?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only on my part but all of the inhabitants of our village. I know my village well. I know the people. Nobody would do a thing like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: But there are no witnesses as to what actually happened; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There aren't. I'm only here to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also testified about the shelling?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that Hamdija Selmic came and said that you should go to Maslovare?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Tell me, on whose behalf was he speaking when he said that you should go to Maslovare?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was sent by Serbs from Maslovare, because his house was right next to Maslovare. He had surrendered of his own accord and the Serbs told him, "Go to Blagaj and tell the people to evacuate to the adjacent village of Maslovare." So he passed through the entire Blagaj, reached my hamlet, and told us, "I was given an order to tell you this, and will you please pick up your things and go?"

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: He wasn't more specific as to who gave him that order?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He didn't name any names but he said it was the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You then described your trip to Maslovare, your journey. Tell me, how is it possible for you to be put up in Maslovare? Where did the original, inhabitants go?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We stayed with a man, Rajko Hodzic, who was extremely rich. He had a huge stable holding 100 to 200 calves. We slept in that stable, in trailers. We were put up in doors, inside the house. It was a huge holding with huge barns and stables.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And again, we come to the surrendering of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said 20 rifles and 20 hunting rifles?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, plus about 20 pistols, all that we had, all that the inhabitants had, but all of these were licensed weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned two names here, Mica Karlica and Milan Gvozden?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, Milan Gvozden.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who are these people?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are Serbs, both of them went to school together with me, same class. They held no rank. They only wore uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And after that, they told you to go back home?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they entered the village, searched houses, hoisted the flags, they told us we were free to go back but not to dare take the flags down. If anybody should take the flag down, they would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I assume it's the same group of armed people, including this Gvozden person, this Karlica, and the others? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the same people. They did not mistreat us up there. They didn't do us any harm. I have to be honest.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Then you mentioned again the negotiations held with the Serbs over 17 days, according to what you said?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us who was leading those negotiations at this point?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What point?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Well, after you came back to your village.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who headed the negotiations? Sifet for the most part from Suhaca. I can't remember his last name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mean Barjaktarevic?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Sifet Barjaktarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And from the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I never spoke to the man. I never asked Sifet who he was talking to and where he was going.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know what options were on the table in those negotiations, who was offering what?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I know that our side was willing, since we had already surrendered our weapons, to continue living in our homes. We were negotiating about being able to continue our life at home, to be left alone, but I don't know where and how the negotiations were headed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You then described an event where Sulejman Burzic was killed. Can you tell me if your memory is now refreshed? Who was it exactly who killed him?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name Janjetovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said Zare Janjetovic from Svodna; that's what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true. Then years went by and you don't remember everything with the same clarity. He was the secretary of the local commune in the village of Svodna.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, you said that this Janjetovic person kicked him from the back?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not from the back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How was it?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were facing each other, and Janjetovic hit him with a rifle, hitting his umbrella. He dropped the umbrella, after which Janjetovic fired two bullets into him and shot him in the chest, shot him dead, in front of all the refugees who were watching this scene from behind the fence, the barbed -- the wire fence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Tell me, before you entered the compound of this enterprise, you described how those three citizens were killed, the men whose names you found in the record of exhumation?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whom do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mehmedagic, Fehim; Camil Alic; and the third person. They were killed by Dragan Balaban, according to your statement.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, nicknamed Trnka. He shot them with a burst of gunfire in the back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You knew those three men who were killed at that spot?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Camil is my cousin.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You know also Dragan Balaban?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I know him from Bosanski Novi. He worked at the bus station. He went to the reserve drills with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You then described how you were loaded on to rail cars. You said there were about 10 to 15 rail cars?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't count them. I didn't matter to me. It was a whole train. I suppose there were about 10 to 15 rail cars.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If we should now compare the number of rail cars of about 20, let's say, with the possible number of people per rail car, you said about 100, if you put 100 people in a rail car, it would be packed, we would get a much smaller figure than the one you gave.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know to what extent the other rail cars were packed. I know what the situation was in my rail car. There were all sorts of rail cars, including the open-type ones. It is possible that they put more people in closed rail cars than in the -- and put the rest in the open rail cars.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: As you were entering rail cars, as you were getting in, who was securing your entrance as you were coming in? Who was guarding you?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Reservists, troops, the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Does that army include your local reservists whom you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mico Dolic, for instance, lives also in Blagaj. I asked him. It was him I asked whether I can board the same rail car as my family, and he nodded. He was drinking coffee. I saw him in the rain drinking this coffee and he nodded that I could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was anyone resisting getting on to the rail car?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody wanted to -- nobody resisted. We all wanted to leave, even I was praying to God that I should leave, that I should be allowed to go because we couldn't take it any longer. I realised we couldn't go on living there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At one point you said that you, who were inside the rail car, closed the door.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said we closed the rail car door when Hasan was killed, because we had small children with us who were watching these killings and we were afraid that there would be more killings and we didn't want the children to go on watching that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Does that mean that the door wasn't locked during your journey?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They weren't locked at that point. Whether they locked them later, I don't know. Whether they locked the doors after they closed all the doors on all the rail cars, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also said that you stopped at one point and drank water from a creek.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a place, Stanari, outside Doboj, a very small settlement, a small railway station where we were separated, men were separated from women and children. It was hot in the rail cars. Women got out to that creek to change the clothes of children, have water.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you also guarded there?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by both police and the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When did these police first appear in Stanari?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you mean military police or the normal police in blue uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean military police, and the army, soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In that place, in Stanari, where you were separated from women and children, is that the same group of soldiers who guarded you as you were boarding the rail -- the train?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That previous group of soldiers was left behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So we now have a different unit, different military unit?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so. It must have been prearranged by telephone or whatever. It must have been agreed in advance who would meet us up at that next railway station.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you men were returned to Novi and put up at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You didn't know at that point what was going on with the women and the children?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you later met -- reunited with your wife, what did she tell you about what happened to them?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were taken to Doboj and then on, through Slavonska Pozega, eventually reaching Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So they continued their journey?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I repeat my answer again?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'll repeat my question: The women and the children continued their journey after being separated from you and ended up in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Whereas you arrived at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where exactly were you accommodated?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: During daytime, in the field of the stadium, and during the night, under the stands.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show this witness the photograph of the stadium which is an exhibit, 1683.3. Here we see the building and the stands?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When you say, "Under the stands," do you mean the premises, the windows of which we see on this picture, facing opposite the field?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not these ones but on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you were indoors?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see this glass here? There was one exit here. It was locked. We couldn't use it. There were two or three rooms upstairs here and elderly people were put up there because there was carpeting of some sorts and it was warmer so they were put up up there and we younger people were on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And it was from there that you tried to send a message?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the people from upstairs who saw the UN troops through the window, flashing their lights at them, and they tried to respond, making signs to signal their presence, using clothes, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: There were locker rooms, massage rooms, as usual, at stadiums, possibly a canteen?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all the usual premises, locker rooms, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: All that was available for your use?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there any other refugees put up at that stadium, in addition to you?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Where could you put up refugees here? The people who lived here, there were people who normally lived in these apartments. They might be living there still for all I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Here, upstairs?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And when you were describing how you were filling in this form that you were leaving Bosanski Novi of your own free will, signing away your property, you said some civilians had come, up -- put up desks at the stadium, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: But the form on your behalf was brought there by your cousin already signed?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you didn't have to sign right there at the stadium? You could have signed elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I couldn't go to the municipality and get my own papers. She did that for me. She signed for me there, and right there, we had to sign in our own hand because not everybody had a relative like I did. Whoever had family to do the paperwork for them did so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Let me get this clear. She got the form for you?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's request, could we please slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment. Please slow down again.

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm finished. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Trbojevic. Is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I have a few questions for you, Mr. Alic, more or less clarifications, because there is a considerable confusion that has been created as a result of too many Balabans. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm referring you specifically to the description that you gave of the killing of Camil Alic, Fehim Mehmedagic, and Samir Izmirevic. More are less you did clarify who exactly did the killing a few minutes ago, and I'm referring everyone to page 27, line 16, and you referred to the person who killed these -- who shot these persons, these three Muslims, as Dragan Balaban, also known as Trnka. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm saying this because earlier on today, on page 6, line 7, you -- the transcript tells us that you referred to this person who did the killing, according to you, as Branko Balaban. It was not Branko Balaban but it was Dragan Balaban. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Slavenko Balaban. Slavenko Balaban nicknamed Sinter, that's another person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait a minute, I'm referring you only to the killing of Camil Alic, Fehim Mehmedagic, and Samir Izmirevic. Who did that killing?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean Besirevic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Not Besirevic. Samir Izmirevic, Fehim Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mehmedagic, and Camil Alic. Who killed those three Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago Balaban nicknamed Trnka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm asking you this and I'm asking a confirmation of you because on page 6 line 7 of the transcript, you don't mention or the transcript does not mention Drago or Dragan Balaban but Branko Balaban. So it's not Branko Balaban who killed these three Muslims. It's Dragan, Dragan Balaban?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. The same mistake recurs in yesterday's transcript and I'm referring you to page 13.886, line 18, where the transcript says that "the person who killed Camil Alic, Fehim Mehmedagic and Samir Izmirevic is Branko Balaban called Sice." Is that correct or is it a mistake? The person who killed these three persons, Camil Alic, Fehim Mehmedagic, and Samir Izmirevic, is it Branko Balaban called Sice or Dragan Balaban known as Trnka?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drago Balaban, also known as Trnka, T-r-n-k-a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and in confirmation of that, just for the record, I mentioned that on page 6 of this statement of the witness given on 12/3/2000, he does refer as the person who killed these three Muslims being Dragan Balaban, and in his statement of the 8th of December, 1997, he refers to also to Drago Balaban, known as Trnka. Is there a distinction between Dragan and Drago or is it the same name?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Also in the statement of 15/1/1998, he refers to Drago Balaban, known as Trnka, as the person who killed these three Muslims. Now, in your statements and in your testimony, you also mention other Balabans. In your statement of 1998, 11 December, 1998, you refer to a certain Ranko Balaban, who according to you was the President of the SDS in Bosanski Novi. You then refer to another Ranko Balaban, as one of the guards in the stadium. Are these the same person? Is this the same person? Or are they two different persons with the same name?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's one person but that Slavenko Balaban, who killed my brother, Camil -- and Kemal -- nicknamed Sinter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will come to Slavenko Balaban later. For the time being, I'm referring to you a different name, not Slavenko Balaban but Ranko Balaban. What was the name of the president of the SDS in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The President of the SDS? Well, I don't know what his name was. I know who was the President -- who was the mayor, that is to say, but as to the party, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In your statement to the Prosecution of March 2000 -- he mentions Balaban as the President of the SDS. Was there a certain Ranko, Ranko Balaban, president of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ranko can only be Gvozden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, one moment. Any way, let's have the break and I will come back to you with the references, because you refer to a certain Ranko Balaban and we want to know exactly who he is. Let's have a 25-minute break, which is overdue in any case and try to remember who was in the meantime Milan Balaban; Ranko Balaban; and Balaban, Slavenko. Balaban, Slavenko, we need to ask you about because he is supposedly the one who killed your brother, amongst other people. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would like to be excused for the balance of the session because I have other --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Ackerman, I understand Mr. Trbojevic will be taking over?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, and I will see you all again next Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have a safe journey and we hope you will be all right when you get back.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I was asking you a few questions, and I have got very few of them left. You also mentioned Balaban Slavenko. This was the one who was nicknamed Sice, no?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sinter. That was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sinter?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Siter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he used to work in Bosanski Novi. He was a waiter there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the time he, according to you, killed your brother and your brother-in-law, what was he wearing? Civilian clothes or military clothes? Or a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wearing a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What kind of uniform?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Camouflage, a camouflage military uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. And the other Dragan Balaban, Trnka, who killed, according to you, the other persons, Camil Alic and the other two, what was he wearing when he killed them?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same as Slavenko, exactly the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you know of certain Ranko Balaban, who was the President of the SDS in Josava?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've remembered him. Yes, his name was Ranko Balaban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in the course of these events that you described to us?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see him in those days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Was there a relationship, a family relationship, between Slavenko Balaban and Drago Balaban? Were they related?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the same family, Slavenko, Drago, and Ranko, they were close relatives from the same village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That means they were also related to the President of the SDS from Josava?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know of a certain Milan Balaban?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in the course of these events?

utterances.speaker: MIDHO ALIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. That brings us to the end of your testimony. On behalf of the Tribunal, it is my duty to thank you for having accepted to come over and give evidence in this trial. You will now be attended to by the officials of this Tribunal to assist you on your return to your country of residence. The usher will be escorting you out. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, meanwhile, I would like to tender officially into evidence the two new documents which I used with this witness, P1627 and P1628.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. There are so being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, I suppose that the officers of this Tribunal who are in charge will bring in the screen and let me explain to the public and the gallery what's going to happen because I don't want to disappoint anyone. The next witness that we will be starting with has asked for certain protective measures, as a result of which we have decided to give him two protective measures. One is he will not be referred to by name but by a nom de plume, by a pseudonym, and that means that you will not be able to see him, although you will be able to hear him, and also, we will be giving him image distortion. So what you will be seeing on the screen over there is the distortion of the image of this testimony. For the time being, we are putting down the curtains, unless he walks in. Then we will pull the curtains up again and you can follow the proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, at the very beginning I'd ask to go briefly into private session just for some background questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. And, Chuqing, please make sure that the monitors and -- first that the screen is put at an angle which does obstruct every possible vision of -- field of view, that could expose the identity of the witness. I think that's -- that should be good. The important thing is, usher, that anyone who goes to the far end of the gallery will not be able to see the -- but I think, as it is, it should be all right. Because we had several members of the gallery yesterday trying to do precisely that, young girls and young boys that were too curious, as if it was going to change anything for them. Yes, please bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are about to start giving evidence in the trial instituted by this Tribunal against Radoslav Brdjanin. Our rules require that any witness, before starting his or her evidence, makes -- enters a solemn declaration to the effect that he or she will be telling the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth in the course of the testimony. The text of the solemn declaration which is tantamount to an oath is contained on a piece of paper which the usher has just handed to you. Your responsibility, your duty, is to read that statement aloud, and that will be your undertaking with this Tribunal that you will be speaking the truth and nothing but the truth. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, you may sit down. You are going to be handed a piece of paper now which contains your name and surname. I want you to have a look at it and without reading it, tell us, please, whether your name and surname appears on that sheet of paper and whether they are spelled correctly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Usher, please show it to the Defence counsel and then to us. And that's going to be entered into the exhibits under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: P1629, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: P1629. Now, very briefly, sir, what's going to happen is this: First of all, you have asked for and we have decided to give you some precautionary, some protective measures to hide your identity. That should make you feel more comfortable and more secure in the course of your testimony. We are trying to protect you because you sought such protection. The protection that we have given to you, protective measures are two. Basically we will not be referring to you by your name and surname but by a number that we have given you and you are BT84 -- am I correct? 82? BT82. You are BT82. And in addition, no one will be able to see you or see your face, because, as you are able to see yourself on the video mode on your monitor, we have provided for a visual distortion of your face. So basically, anyone following these proceedings will be able to hear you giving testimony but will not be able to see your face. Now, Mr. Julian Nicholls for the Prosecution will be putting some questions to you in chief, and for the first part, since he will be asking you your name, your surname, your place of birth, your age and whatever, we are going to go into private session. In other words, for this short interval of time, until we finish with this series of questions, no one will be able to follow the proceedings. No one will be able to hear your voice. So, Mr. Nicholls, please let's go into private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we are in open session now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness please have the map of the area, P1624?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, please remember while we are getting the map that -- not to say your own name, not to say the names of family members who also doing so might identify you.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know if we can zoom in a tiny bit to make this more clear. That's good. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Witness, sir, if you could look at this map, please, see if it looks accurate to you, reasonably accurate, and point out the village of Suhaca on the map.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. It is correct, and this is the village of Suhaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And is the map correct in showing the location of Suhaca in relationship to the town of Bosanski Novi and Blagaj Japra?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to briefly ask you if you could tell me about what relations were like in the Suhaca area which you've pointed out to us before the war in Croatia. If you -- you can correct me if I'm wrong but before the war in Croatia, really got under way, relationships between the Serbs and Muslims in that area were generally good. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. The relations were very good indeed. We used to play soccer together. We used to get together and socialise, both in Suhaca and Josava.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And Josava, excuse my pronunciation, is a Serb village. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes, it is an exclusively Serb village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And if you can tell me briefly how these relationships changed during the war with Croatia. In your statement you refer to that's when problems started.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. From the very start of the war in Croatia, they started to separate from us, they didn't want to talk to us. And later on, they even refused to play soccer with us on a number of occasions, so we got the idea that something was going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And just to be clear, when you say "they" in that answer, who are you referring to? We need to be clear for the record and the transcript.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: What I mean is the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During this time, were you personally active in politics? Were you a member of any party? Did you run for any office?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. I wasn't involved in politics and I wasn't a member of anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Which party represented Suhaca, which party was the majority party in Suhaca?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: The SDA party.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And speaking now in early 1992, who was president of the SDA in Suhaca?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: It was Sifet Barjaktarevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If you know, can you just tell me, if you remember, who other senior SDA members were in the municipality of Bosanski Novi as a whole? If you remember their names.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: There were Mr. Resad Berberovic, and Dzafer -- I can't remember his family name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. Although you weren't politically too active in politics, did you follow what was going on in the news, on the television, and in the media, newspapers, magazines?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes, I did, because that was the main topic of every day, the events in the neighbouring Croatia and in the neighbouring area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During 1992, was there a point where the broadcasts you were able to receive on television stopped? Were there any channels which stopped being broadcast? Was your selection limited in any way?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. It wasn't limited. We had three programmes that we could watch.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Around this time, when you said that the relationships were becoming difficult, were breaking down, were any patrols set up to -- in Suhaca village, to make it safe at night?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. There were no organised patrols in Suhaca. There were just a couple of policemen as required by the municipality of Bosanski Novi, as reserve policemen.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During 1992, if you remember, was there any time in Suhaca and in Bosanski Novi in general where Muslims began to be dismissed from their employment, when they were fired?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. It did happen, and Muslims were being dismissed during the war in Croatia, as early as that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell me how you know that, what the basis of your knowledge is for that, for those dismissals?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I know it because my cousin was a civil servant at the municipality and he was dismissed. A neighbour of mine was a driver for the municipal authorities and that happened to him as well and I know a policeman who was dismissed as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were Serbs also dismissed at this time?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can you give me an approximate time frame of when these dismissals began to take place.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: The dismissals started, as I said, in the course of the war in Croatia, and then right into the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. You also spoke in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor about checkpoints being set up which controlled the movement of Muslims and prevented Muslims from travelling at night. Could you describe that to the Trial Chamber, please, when those checkpoints were set up and who, as far as you know, was in charge of those checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: The checkpoints were set up at some point in April 1992, and they were manned by the JNA soldiers, only of Serb nationality, and I myself had my documents checked at those checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were Serbs also required to show identification at these checkpoints and have their movement restricted?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. They weren't required to show anything. The day when my papers were checked, I had even one Serb accompanying me in order to tell them to let me through. They didn't ask anything of him but they said that they would check me nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you indicate, please, on the map which is to your right, approximately where the checkpoints were around Suhaca?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I can. One checkpoint was between Hozici and Donji Agici. And another checkpoint was between Suhaca and Josava, near the elementary school in Suhaca, right here.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. And these are checkpoints which you personally witnessed or ones which you heard about? You told of being stopped at one checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: These are the checkpoints which I saw with my own eyes and where I had my papers checked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I now want to move on to talk about the topic of the surrender of weapons from the village of Suhaca. You speak about that in your statement. I wonder if you can tell us how -- how you -- how people in Suhaca first learned that they were going to be required to surrender all rifles, pistols, and other weapons that they may have had.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Sifet Barjaktarevic was the President of the SDA and he was often called to the municipality for negotiations. One day he came to us and said, "People, we reached an agreement of this sort. If we surrender our weapons, that will mean that we are loyal to the Serbian authorities and we will be allowed to go on living as before." So we collected our weapons and complied.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Let me take this step by step. When did you first hear about this demand or this agreement?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: In the end April.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know who Sifet Barjaktarevic spoke to, who he negotiated with, to come to this agreement?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I don't know exactly who he talked to but he went to the Bosanski Novi municipality and I later heard that even -- he even went to Banja Luka a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
