utterances.text: Let me see if I can help you remember. In your statement, on page 3, and I can show it to you if you need it, you speak about Sifet Barjaktarevic discussing the problem of surrender, the surrender of weapons with Ranko Balaban of Josava. Do you remember that name, Ranko Balaban?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes, that name is very familiar. Ranko Balaban also went to Bosanski Novi for these negotiations together with Sifet Barjaktarevic. Of course, he couldn't decide alone either. It had to be decided in Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what position did Ranko Balaban hold? Who was he?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Ranko Balaban was the President of the Josava SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So the discussions between your representative, just to be very clear, Sifet Barjaktarevic, was with Ranko Balaban and other members of the SDS. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: That's correct. All that came down from the Bosanski Novi municipality went through Ranko Balaban, who informed Sifet that he was to go there for negotiations, and then they went to Bosanski Novi together.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were these weapons ultimately surrendered by people in Suhaca?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. It was surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And just to be clear, what was the ethnic composition of the village of Suhaca?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: The village of Suhaca was purely Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell me simply how the weapons were actually turned over, how this exchange took place?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: The next day, after these negotiations, Sifet Barjaktarevic convened in meeting in Suhaca and told everyone they had to bring all their weapons they had. And we complied. We put all the weapons on to a tractor-trailer, made a list, it was mainly hunting weapons. We loaded them on to this tractor-trailer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you personally surrender any weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. I never possessed a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who picked up the weapons? You say you loaded them on a tractor-trailer, who came and took these weapons away?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: It was our tractor and our man drove the tractor in front of us, and we accompanied him out of the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I guess my question is: Do you know ultimately who took custody of these weapons, who they were surrendered to? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: The weapons were taken over by the Serbs at that checkpoint between Suhaca and Josava. Where these weapons ended up, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And were those Serbs in charge of the checkpoint soldiers or police or civilians?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: They wore military uniforms and they called themselves the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During this time period, do you know whether Serb villages, such as Josava, were also disarmed in a similar manner?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. They were not. They even received new weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How do you know that? Could you explain, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I know that because I saw with my own eyes, a helicopter landing in the hamlet of Halilovici.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And why does that helicopter landing lead you -- could you explain further, please. Why does that mean that weapons were being distributed?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I can explain. After the landing of that helicopter, two civilian vehicles passed by driven by Serbs, men I know personally, and half an hour later, the vehicles came back loaded with weapons. They were slightly covered by blankets but you could still see the weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who was driving these vehicles, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I can. The red Wartburg was driven by Mijo Majkic and there was another Lada driven by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could I ask to you repeat the name, please, of the person who was driving the Lada?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The person driving the Lada was Podunavac, that's his last name but I'm not sure if it's Ranko or Radenko -- or rather Dragan Podunavac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, after this negotiation to surrender weapons and everybody in Suhaca agreed and did in fact surrender their weapons in order to hopefully live in peace, what happened after that, in the following days?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: The day when we surrendered our weapons, all the inhabitants had to go to the village of Josava for a such which lasted for three or four hours, returned home this same day and at this checkpoint we were told we would be able to live in peace from then on. In fact, the first shell hit us a couple of days later.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: All right. And when you talk about a search in your last answer, are you talking about a search of the homes in the village of Suhaca?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. They were searching our houses, which we had to leave unlocked.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And again, who was searching the houses, if you know? Who was actually physically conducting the searches?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Those were soldiers, JNA soldiers, accompanied by two Muslim civilians from Suhaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And during these searches, was any property damaged or was anything stolen or were the searches done correctly?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: The searches were done correctly. Nothing was taken away or stolen that day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, I interrupted you, but you were talking about how a couple of days later, the first shell hit. Can you tell me now how the shelling of Suhaca started and what that first day of shelling was like.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Three days after the surrendering of weapons, the first shell landed. It was around 6.30. We were taken aback. It was one of the worst days. They shelled the whole day and the whole night, I believe. In the days that followed, the shelling took place only in the early morning hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Could you tell where these shells were coming from, where they were being fired from?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I can. The shells were coming from the villages of Josava and Krslje.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I think you talk in your statement about how you examined one of these shells and using your military background, you thought you were able to tell what type of shell it was. Can you explain that to the Court, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: One of the shells landed not far from my house. I went there. I dug out the so-called tail of the shell. The tail fin. I saw the writing "JNA" on it. It was a 60-millimetre calibre shell.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned the village of Krslje. Was that a Serb or a Muslim village?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: It was a purely Serb village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long, in terms of days, did the shelling last of Suhaca?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: The shelling lasted four to five weeks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did the intensity of the shelling vary during those weeks?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. It varied. Sometimes a day would pass without a single shell being fired. Sometimes they shelled mainly in the early morning hours. At night, a couple of shells, around noon.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what did you and the other people who were in the village at that time do to cope with that? What did you try to hide or get away or do anything to protect yourselves?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. We tried. We spent most of the time in so-called shelters. We lived in old houses mainly with stone basements and all the inhabitants would gather in one or two houses with women and children staying inside, and men making rounds outside to prevent anyone from entering the village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: At this point, you say there were men outside trying to prevent anyone from entering the village. Did these men have any weapons or any arms?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. They were not armed. In fact, at that time, they didn't have any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And just before we move on, can you tell me, tell the Court about any damage done by this shelling? What was the effects of this shelling?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Shelling mainly targeted the parts of the hamlets where the mosques were, and it was mainly houses around the mosques that were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How did this shelling come to end? Tell me about how this -- how -- at the end of these weeks, what happened? What happened when the shelling stopped?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: As I already said, shelling was less intensive during the day, and every time the shelling stopped, a military vehicle would come in and they asked what was going on. One day, they came again. They said they couldn't entrust security to us, that the army was coming, the so-called Hurde. That we had it retreat towards Bosanski Novi where it would be decided where we were to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: All right. So the military told you that they could not protect you and you were -- and that Suhaca was about to be attacked. Is that right? And that you had to leave, everybody had to leave?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Other than what you said, that during the shelling men would walk around the village to try to prevent anyone from entering, was there any organised military action or any organised defence in Suhaca during that shelling and during the period just before the shelling?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. There was no organised defence in Suhaca at all, nothing in military terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness P1653, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document, I think you looked at the other day. Unfortunately, it's undated, review of security/relevant information for Bosanski Novi municipality. If you look at the second paragraph of the document, the second sentence says, "The extremist part of the SDA party, Party of Democratic Action has proceeded to issue arms on a massive scale to citizens of Muslim ethnicity, prepared primarily to executes any tasks entrusted to them by the SDA." And then if you look on page 2, in the B/C/S version, item number 3, it describes Suhaca village in these terms: "Sifet Barjaktarevic is in charge of all activities. It is in this village that activity it is the most organised, both paramilitary and every other kind." And then it states that in the last world war, Suhaca was a prominent Ustasha strong hold. My question very simply is: Is there any truth at all to what's stated in this document about Suhaca and about the SDA arming Muslims to do its bidding, especially in the village of Suhaca?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. There isn't any truth in that. There were no organisations at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Briefly, what kind of man was Sifet Barjaktarevic? Did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I did. He was one of the better people I can say in the whole valley of Japra. He helped youth centre and a sports centre be built there. He did a lot for the youth and for the sports, mainly football.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'd like to come back to the day you told us about where the military JNA came and told you and the people of Suhaca that they had to leave. Can you tell me what happened after you were told that, how many people from the village left, how they tried to leave, what they could bring with them.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: On that day, when we departed from Suhaca, we set off, all of us, taking whatever we could.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how many people was that, do you estimate, from Suhaca?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Men, women and children, totalling about 1200.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there Muslim men, women and children from other villages around Suhaca leaving at the same time?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. On the same day, all the villages set off from Gornji Agici, Donji Agici, Crna Rijeka, all the way up to Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how was this transport? Were people walking? In cars? How did people leave?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Mainly in cars, tractors, horse-drawn carts, whatever people had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And approximately once all the people from all these villages had started to leave, how many people in total do you think were trying to leave the valley on that day?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Somewhere between 8.000 and 10.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And do you remember what day this was, what the date was, that this huge convoy left?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: It was the 24th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the map again, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, when you set out, you and the members of your village on the 24th of May, from Suhaca, can you just indicate with the pointer what the route you planned to take was, how you proposed to go and where you thought you were going to travel to?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. I can show, because Sifet Barjaktarevic had said that he would manage to talk to the authorities in Bosanski Novi to get them to let us through from Suhaca, through Blagaj Japra, in the direction of Bosanski Novi and then across the Una to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know which authorities he was talking to, to negotiate this mass movement of people, who he was talking to in Bosanski Novi?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you've shown us the proposed route. Tell us what happened. Were you able to go as you hoped and reach Bosanski Novi that day?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. We didn't, because at Blagaj Japra we were met by the JNA soldiers at the bridge, and they said we couldn't go on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can you describe that encounter a little bit more, please. Why did they say that you couldn't go on and what did the soldiers do?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, well, I was driving a tractor and I managed to cross the bridge and straight after the bridge, there was the railway and there were railway carriages there, and they asked us to leave all our property and to board the carriages and we disagreed, and then they told us to turn back to the village of Blagaj, and so that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And now this isn't just you but everybody who was trying to leave, is that right, or did some people make it through with their cars or tractors?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. Nobody managed to get through on that day. We were all turned back to the village of Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you just tell me how you know that these were -- I think you said JNA soldiers who stopped you at the bridge.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: According to their uniforms. They all wore JNA uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, once you and these thousands of other people crossed the bridge back to Blagaj Japra, what happened there? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: We returned to Blagaj Japra and then we were looking for the people we knew who could allow us to stay at their houses and wait to see what happened because we couldn't go back to Suhaca. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, did everybody that you know make it back across the bridge and make it safely to Blagaj Japra or was anybody detained out of the crowd?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. Everybody could go back on that day, and we all stayed at the village of Blagaj Japra.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I may not be -- I may have not understood. In your statement, you talk about two brothers, Nijaz and Karanfil Isakovic. Can you tell me if anything happened to them? Maybe I have the date wrong.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: It was 17 days later when we made a second attempt to cross the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. Can you tell me -- you just said 17 days. Can you tell me about those 17 days in Blagaj Japra. What was there to eat and where did you sleep? You said that people tried to stay with people they knew, but was there enough accommodation for all of the people in the convoy?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No, there wasn't enough accommodation for all. I was sleeping in a garage, and in the same house, in the courtyard, there was my -- the rest of my family, my wife and my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what went on during these 17 days? Was there any attempt to negotiate a solution to the problem so that you and the other people could bring your tractors and property with you and not abandon it all at the bridge?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. We took them back to the village of Blagaj and then Sifet was engaged in talks with them and he insisted on the fact that we should be allowed to go to Croatia and they refused.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know if any other community leaders also negotiated along with Sifet, and I take it you mean Sifet Barjaktarevic?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. No. Whenever it was about any sort of negotiations, they always asked for Sifet Barjaktarevic. There were a couple of other men who had the right to accompany him for talks to Bosanski Novi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And in Bosanski Novi, do you know which authorities, Mr. Barjaktarevic negotiated with, whether they were military or civilian or both? Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I don't know. I just simply know that he went for talks to Bosanski Novi. When he came back, he didn't want to create panic. He just said, "I have to go back for further talks tomorrow. They don't want us to go in the direction of Croatia and we'll see about the rest." He kept referring to "them." I don't know who he meant exactly, the army or what.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And was Mr. Barjaktarevic successful in negotiating a reasonable solution to this problem?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No, he wasn't successful.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what happened after those 17 days, if you could describe what ended that 17 day block of time?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: On the 17th day, at about 10.00 in the morning, a bus full of soldiers drove through the village of Blagaj and then a truck, a tank and a blue golf of the Belgrade television station.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Straight after the village of Blagaj, in the so-called Troske village, they stopped and soldiers were getting off the bus and the tank was turned in the direction of Blagaj. We could see it with my own -- with our own eyes. The soldiers surrounding the village and then they started shooting at about 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What were they shooting with? Are you talking about shelling or shooting with rifles, the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: The way -- using guns only. I believe that the tank was there for intimidation purposes only.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And was there any shelling of Blagaj Japra on this day, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Not on that day but before, in the course of these 17 days, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who were the targets of this shooting, just to be very clear? Who were the soldiers shooting at?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: They were shooting upon the civilians only, and that's how they created all this panic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And then what happened -- how long after that shooting did this attack on the civilians at Blagaj, how long did it last?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: At around 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So for about two hours?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. About two hours, until everybody came out on to the road and then again, in the direction of the bridge in Blagaj Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can you describe how everybody went towards the bridge and how they tried to escape. Can you describe that in a little more detail. You said there was a panic starting. Can you try to describe the scene at the bridge to the Chamber?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. There was a lot of panic. People started fleeing in all directions, but they were always turned back by soldiers and we were only allowed to go across the bridge in the direction of Blagaj Rijeka. Then we were met by soldiers at the bridge and they were searching us and we were required to leave everything we had, money, jewellery, IDs, the car papers, keys. They were especially pleased with the car keys.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think this is pretty obvious but you said that one of the big disputes in the beginning was whether or not you'd be able to bring cars and tractors and property with you across the bridge. Was anybody allowed to bring any personal property that you know of across the bridge? You've talked about this search but was anybody allowed to bring a car or anything else?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. Nobody was allowed to carry even a shopping bag, let alone anything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was taken from you personally, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I had a couple of photos from when I was a soldier, some money, and a watch.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did men and women cross this bridge together, did families cross it together, or were people separated in any way?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Initially they were crossing together, up until the so-called Zoran red beret arrived, and then he was separating women from the men, the women on the right and the men on the left. And that's how we were crossing the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were any people who were crossing the bridge, were there any wounded from the shooting which you described earlier? Were there any wounded people trying to cross the bridge?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. There were two wounded people, and they were wounded by some special bullets.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said Zoran with the red beret arrived. Do you know Zoran's last name?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. I don't. I only heard that he was from the village of Dobrljina in the direction of Bosanska Kostajnica. He was wearing a red beret and that's what people called him, "Red beret."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was he wearing a uniform in addition to the red beret? Do you remember what type of uniform he was wearing, if any?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. A military SMB uniform of the JNA army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, I asked you earlier about the Isakovic brothers, and I think I got the date wrong. Can you tell me if it was on this day, what happened to them, to Nijaz and Karanfil?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. On that day, when we were crossing the bridge, on the 9th of June, the two Izakovic brothers, Nijaz and Karanfil, were standing on the left side of the bridge and they were -- their heads hanging and their hands were tied by a wire.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who did this to them? Who did this to these brothers? Who tied them up like that?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I didn't see that because when I was crossing the bridge, they were already tied up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you ever see these two brothers again, after that day, on the 9th of June?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No, never again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You didn't know this soldier, Zoran. Did you recognise any soldiers that day as you were crossing the bridge, anybody who you had known personally?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Soldier Zoran I did not know, as you yourself mentioned, and I didn't know the two soldiers searching me either. I mean, but one of them was at school with me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long did it take to cross the bridge, for everyone to cross the bridge?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: It took between four and five hours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was on the other side of the bridge? What was waiting for you and all the other people from your village and the other villages?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: On the other side of the bridge, there were other soldiers waiting for us, and they were herding us on to the premises of the Japra company and then we were searched again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: We'll get to what happened inside the Japra company in a minute. But up to this point, had you seen anybody, any other crimes being committed, others than the robbery of civilians trying to cross the bridge?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. When the panic broke out and people ran out of the houses on to the main road, and in the direction of the bridge, I didn't see it myself with my own eyes, but other people who were running along with me, they told me that three people, as many as three people, had already been killed in the hamlet of Sikare.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, once you crossed to the other side, can you describe how you were -- in just a little bit more detail, how you were taken and placed in the Japra factory? Japra company factory?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. As we were crossing the bridge, they were directing us to the premises of the company. It was surrounded by barbed wire. And then we were sitting inside, and then it started to rain. There was heavy rain and so people were running inside to shelter from the rain.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And at this point, did you see anybody separated from the crowd and mistreated in any way?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. A soldier came along in civilian car. He entered and he started beating people and chasing them out, and so he chased all the men outside and allowed the women and children to be inside, to shelter from the rain. In the course of all that, he came across a man and he asked him, "Do you know me?" And the guy answered yes. And then he turned around and shot him. He shot him in the stomach.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you ask him directly whether he knows who this soldier, the name of the soldier who came in this civilian car and who allegedly shot this other man? And whether he knows the name of this other man who was shot?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's just where I was going, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the soldier who committed this crime? The name of the person?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The person who was killed is called Husein Burzic, and the soldier who killed him is Dragan. He was in a village of Svodna and he was a registrar [Realtime transcript read in error "registered"] there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: He was registered there. Do you know what his position was there in the village of Svodna?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: He was a registrar there, not registered. He worked at the municipal offices of the Svodna village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Was -- it did he occupy any position in the SDS of that village?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. Do you know if this man Dragan occupied a position with the SDS in that village?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I didn't know him in person. I just saw him on that occasion, and he was wearing military uniform.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that the name of the man who was murdered was Husein Burzic. In your statement, you talk about the murder of Sulejman Burzic. Can you tell me which the correct name is?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I do apologise. I may have made a mistake. The correct name is Sulejman Burzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to what you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Let's clear this up, because in his statement to the Prosecutor, on page 5, third paragraph, second line, when he refers to this man called Dragan, who supposedly committed this murder. He says, "A man named Dragan came in a Lada. He was the President of the SDS in the village of Svodna. He came in and beat everyone that was in his way. He killed a man in front of me." And the man is, as we have been told was Sulejman Burzic. But according to this document, he did tell the officer of the Prosecutor -- Office of the Prosecutor who interviewed him that Dragan was the President of the SDS in the village of Svodna. Did you say, did you tell the interviewing officer that Dragan was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the President of the SDS in Svodna or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't, because I don't know whether he was the President of the SDS or not. I simply know that he worked at the Registrar's office there before the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Continue, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also describe in your statement an incident, a crime committed by a soldier nicknamed Trnka. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. It was a crime committed in the hamlet of Sikare.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you describe -- is that the crime which -- could you describe that, please? Is that the incident you referred to earlier?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. That was the incident. In the state of panic, some people stayed at their houses and then as the soldiers advanced, they were driving them out of their houses and they -- and small groups were being sent in the direction of the bridge, and from those smaller groups of people some people were taken and killed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'd like to return and ask you some more -- a few more questions about what happened in the Japra company. The murder, the shooting of Sulejman Burzic, where did this take place? Was this something that many people would have witnessed?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. It was in the premises of the Japra company, and at least 1.000 people witnessed it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After that incident, this person Dragan left, then what happened? Did anybody else -- did any other officials or military personnel arrive?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. Dragan got into the car and left, and then a military vehicle called Pinzgauer came along and it was carrying soldiers and there was an officer there as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you remember the name of this officer?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. It was captain Bogdan Grab.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And then what happened? What did he do when he arrived?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: When he arrived, he was calling out to people to come forward. None of those people came forward. And then he asked the men to line up and to prepare any documents, any papers, identity papers they might have had.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you remember the names of the people who were called out by Captain Grab?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Could you name them, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: There were Sifet Barjaktarevic; Hasan Ekic, called Hako; and Husein Ekic, called Buzka; and Samir Blagajcevic; Hasan Merzihic; Fikret Hamzagic; Izet Mehmedagic; and I think that was it, those names only.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: None of those men stepped -- those were the only names he called out. None of those men stepped forward. What happened next? Did anybody look for those particular men?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. After the first call, nobody came forward, and then we all had to line up one by one, and as we were coming out, the soldiers were checking our papers and whatever else we may have had. And at that stage, Husein Ekic, called Buzka, came forward of his own accord, as well as Hasan Ekic, called Hako. And then the soldiers put them into that military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I don't know if we are going to break soon, Your Honour, because this wouldn't be a bad time to stop before we go into something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a break of 25 minutes. Do you reckon that you will take the rest of today's sitting -- you require the rest of today's sitting so at least Mr. Trbojevic will know whether he's to start his cross today or Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would think most of it, Your Honour, maybe a few minutes at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Trbojevic, may I ask you how long do you expect your cross to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I haven't had any interpretation. All right. Okay. So you'll tell us when we resume in 25 minutes time. I'm asking because this gentleman ought to know whether he'll be staying here the weekend or whether he is leaving today or tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you check again, please? He's come now? Yes. I apologise for this delay but we had a problem which we had not anticipated, and I hope there will not be a repetition of it because I will have to report it. So, Mr. Nicholls, before you start, with regard to that witness that you mentioned earlier on, the one for whom you pointed out that we require closed session, I don't need to mention the name because otherwise we will have to go into private session, I have checked the decision to which you referred to earlier on, and I'm going to point it out to the Defence. Please refer to the decision handed down by my predecessor, Judge David Hunt, on the 23rd of May, 2001, in which it was decided that the testimony of the witness to whom Mr. Koumjian referred to in closed session or in private session this morning, shall be heard in closed session amongst other things. Okay? So that's settled. Mr. Koumjian -- sorry, not Mr. Koumjian. Mr. Nicholls, please go ahead with your in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I forget, we'll need to reserve, if we may, two or three minutes at the very end for an administrative matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I just want to ask you one question I should have asked you earlier before the break. I asked you about the murders in Sikare and you described them which were committed by somebody named -- with a nickname of Trnka. Do you know Trnka's real name?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It's -- his family name is Balaban. I think Milan Balaban.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when we stopped before the break, you were telling us about the list of names of men that were called out by Captain Bogdan Grab at the Japra company. And you told us it was Sifet Barjaktarevic, and others. Now, Sifet was the SDA president and representative of Suhaca. Can you tell me what positions, if you know, those other men whose names were called out occupied? Were they also sort of community leaders?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Izet Mehmedagic was in Blagaj and Izet Hamzagic for Bozici, they were community leaders there. And the others were no leaders or representatives of any sort.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, what happened next to Hasan Merzihic?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Mr. Grab, when he called people over the loud speaker, well he told them to step forward, and then a man called Dragan Balaban came along. He embraced Sifet and he said, "Sifet, you don't need anything. We know you. We know who you are." He stayed with them. And the rest of us were ordered to run to the carriages. We boarded the carriages and then a soldier was going from one car to the next and he was calling for Hasan once again. Hasan Merzihic, Izet Hamzagic, and Izet Mehmedagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Let me stop you for one moment. You said Dragan Balaban. I believe in your statement it states Ranko Balaban approached at this time and said we foe who you are Sifet. Can you tell me which is correct and in which -- whether it's a mistake in the statement or in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I dealt with the matter in the previous -- with the previous witness as well, because I see some confusion here. Yes, please tell us whether it was the -- in your statement, there is a particular part in which you say, "In the line, Sifet Barjaktarevic, the SDA president, was in front of me. He was approached by the SDS president, Ranko Balaban. He said, 'Sifet you don't have to show us your ID. We know who you are.'" . Was it Ranko Balaban who told him that, the SDS president, or was it Dragan Balaban?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. It was Ranko Balaban, who was the President of SDS in Josava, and that's one and the same man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So let me ask you another question so that we clear this once and for all -- but you did mention Dragan a certain person, the name Dragan Balaban. Did you know anyone by the name of Dragan Balaban or Drago Balaban?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did know him. It was his brother.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And did he have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you know of someone named -- called Dragan Balaban who was referred to as Trnka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was Milan Balaban who was called Trnka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, because in the previous witness, it was Dragan Balaban who was Trnka. So now it's Milan Balaban.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And just, sir, to make it clear, this SDS president, Ranko Balaban, who said, "It's okay Sifet we all know who you are," that's the same Ranko Balaban with whom Sifet Barjaktarevic had negotiated the surrender of weapons in Suhaca. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes, the same man.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for helping clear that up. I'm sorry I interrupted you. What happened --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry I interrupted you. Can you continue and tell us what happened next after Sifet was identified and Hasan Merzihic? What happened next to these two men?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. Hasan Merzihic was taken out of the carriage and he was taken back to the group where Sifet was and the other two were kind of lucky because the soldiers didn't know them personally, so they kept quiet. And then Zoran, called red beret, approached Hasan. He took him in the direction of the bridge, and he killed him there, and I saw it with my own eyes from the carriage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Just briefly, how did -- how did Zoran, whose last name you don't know, kill this man?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: He shot him. He shot several bullets and then as he was falling, he shot him again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what happened to that gentleman who you'd known well, Sifet Barjaktarevic? What did you see happen next with him?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: He was standing with a couple of soldiers in that group, next to the military vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you continue, please?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. And then Zoran came back, approached Sifet, and he took him in the direction of the bridge, and then I could see Sifet explaining something to him, I couldn't hear the conversation obviously. And he brought him to the edge of the bridge, and then he pushed him away, in the direction of the river bank, and then he was shooting at him, but I don't know if he actually managed to shoot him or not. I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: After that incident, after that action you've just described, did you ever see Sifet Barjaktarevic alive again?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No, never again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And just so that we are clear on the scene, when you witnessed these two shootings, the one where you saw Hasan Merzihic actually murdered and then the shooting towards where you'd seen Sifet Barjaktarevic pushed down, where were you at that time? Were you already on a train, in a carriage, or were you waiting to board the train?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I was still -- I was already on the train, in a carriage.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, had anybody told you and the other people where you were going, what was going to happen to you, why you were being put on these trains? Did you have any idea what was in store for you, what the plan was?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. Nobody had told us anything about what would happen, where we were being taken but you could tell by the train that it was going in the direction of Banja Luka, Prijedor, Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could the witness please be shown P1663?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Could you take a moment to look at that document, sir? It's a Red Cross of Bosanski Novi municipality document dated 7th of June, 1992, and it's headed, "Subject, announcement" in my English translation. And I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. think you've seen this document, I think it was shown to you while you were here.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: About halfway through the first paragraph, in the English translation, it states, "Since UNPROFOR did not want to grant even written requests by these people for resettlement and the International Red Cross has stopped working in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the remaining possible destination of their resettlement is Bosnia. This agreement has been reached with representatives of the Autonomous Region of Krajina in Banja Luka." I'm sorry, I should have read above that. "This concerns Muslims from Blagaj." My question is: You said you didn't know at this point where you were going or where you would be taken to. Had anybody told you during those 17 days that there was any agreement or any negotiation to relocate you and the other civilians somewhere in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. In the course of those 17 days, when Sifet was involved in talks, whenever he came back from Bosanski Novi, he always said, "No, I never -- I haven't managed to achieve anything. They are not allowing us to go in the direction of Croatia."

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The third paragraph talks about Muslim extremists hiding in the surrounding woods, around Blagaj, and due to these operations, there was a real danger of some groups getting out of the command and control mechanism and threatening the safety of people in Blagaj. Are you aware of any armed, extremist or otherwise, resistance around the woods of Blagaj at this time?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. There was no armed uprising, no extremists. In fact they used to call us all extremists. There were no groups of that sort at all. Every single inhabitant to the last man was driven away from Blagaj.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you hear about any incidents of resistance or shootings at Serb patrols?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. I did hear rumours about an event along the road from Bosanski Novi to Prijedor, but then the same rumour said that it was an incident that they had staged themselves so as to be able to use it as an excuse, as something that the Muslims from Blagaj had done.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If you look at the fourth paragraph of this Red Cross announcement, it states, "It is proposed that the operation of voluntary resettlement to Banja Luka should continue using their own means of transport or transport organised by the Crisis Staff." This is a silly question but I'll ask it any way. Was there anything voluntary about you boarding this train that you saw was headed towards Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. There was nothing voluntary about it. It was all under the control of the armed forces, and we did as we were told.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Finally, the last paragraph states that -- it's suggested that this convoy be escorted to Banja Luka by the military and on my copy, civilian police. Did you -- were you able to tell whether or not it was military and/or civilian police that were escorting you and the other civilians on this train?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No, we were not escorted. On the way between Prijedor and Banja Luka, even the doors of the carriages were open, and we would close them ourselves because otherwise there was -- it was a bit drafty.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: All right. Other than the men who you've told us about who were separated and one you saw murdered and another one you saw shots being tired towards where he had been, did everybody else get on these trains, on these cattle cars?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody else was taken into the cars, every single one of us, and then the train started.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were men, women and children placed together in the cars now or was there any -- was anybody separated at this point or was --

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: For that stretch, we were all together. Women, children, and men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell me where the train went and where the first stop that you -- that you're aware of took place?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: The train left in the direction of Prijedor and Banja Luka, and we stayed for a while in Prijedor, about half an hour, and I noticed some soldiers wearing helmets around the train, and it said, "Guard 92" on the helmets. After half an hour, we continued our journey and we got to Ostruzna. It is a village near Doboj.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What happened at Ostruzna?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: The train stopped there, and we were sitting in the carriages for about half an hour or an hour, nobody showed up, and so we started getting off of our own accord, and there was a creek nearby, and the women started washing the clothes for the children and using the water in general, and then a soldier came along. He said he was a Jovo from Romania, he nicknamed himself after somebody who was called Jovo from Kozara in the Second World War. So he separated the women and the children, and the women and children were in the first carriages, and then the remaining carriages were filled with men.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was -- you say women and children. What was the age where somebody stopped being a child?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What was the age, I'm sorry, at which somebody stopped being a child for purposes of which wagon they were put in?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: It was mostly boys of 9 years of age, and then all the way to 60. Since we could not all be fitted into those five or six carriages, then there was another group of boys who were taken back to go with the women and children. So basically it was between the ages of 15 and 60.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Just to be clear, did the men who were older than 60 go with the women and children?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. Men also above 60, also went with women and children, and the couple of these went with us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, could you ask him to give us an indication as according to him how many persons were on this train when they left and before the separation of the two genders took place?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, could you tell me your best estimate of how many people boarded this convoy train at the company in Blagaj Japra all the way until this stop in Ostruzna? How many people were on that train?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: All in all, there were about 8.000 people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, once the men and women were separated, by men I mean the men between 15 and 60 and the women, children and older men, is that -- were you separated from anybody in your family at that point?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. They separated me from my wife. Only my brother and I remained.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What happened to the women and children and the older men, after the separation?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: When we were all separated and put on to rail cars, our rail cars were locked, and then they separated one part of the train from the other, women and children were taken to Doboj, and I learned that when I reunited with my wife in Karlovac. At the moment when this part of the train was leaving, I didn't know where they were going.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how long were you and the other men kept locked in these cattle cars?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: All in all, three days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I mean at this point, at Ostruzna after the women and children have been taken away, how long was it before the train moved again and you were brought somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: It lasted two days. It was two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Where did you go next? Where were you brought? Tell me what happened next when the train you were on started moving again. Where did you go from there, leaving Ostruzna?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. After a couple of hours, the train left in the direction of Banja Luka. That is the same direction we came from. It stopped in Banja Luka. It was already around 11.00 p.m., and we spent the night there sleeping in rail cars, mistreated by the soldiers who were shouting profanities, telling us to go to Manjaca, that it was Alija who had this in store for us, that we were balijas, that we were Ustashas and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And how many men do you think were on the train with you at this time, under -- being treated this way?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Between 700 and 730.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And then the next -- well, were you given any food or drink or anything by the time you'd spent the night in Banja Luka on the train?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No, we didn't get anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And where did the train -- you say you spent the night. When did the train leave the next morning and where did it go, leaving Banja Luka now?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Correct. We slept in the train in Banja Luka, and then the next morning, the train moved on towards Bosanski Novi. We stopped at Blagaj where we had departed from, two days previously. We were met there by a policeman whose name I don't know. I know, though, that he had worked at the police station in Bosanski Novi. He allowed two men to get out to fetch some water. While the train was standing, the first two rail cars managed to get some water, but there was not enough time for the rest. The train then reached Bosanski Novi. It stopped at the railway leading to Bosanska Otoka near the Mlakve stadium. Soldiers lined in two rose were waiting for us there. We had to jump out of the rail cars and run across the road to the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If you remember, do you know what the date was now when you've arrived all the way back in Bosanski Novi and enter the Mlakve stadium?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes, it was the 11th of June, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And again, when you entered the stadium, did anybody tell you -- did any of the soldiers tell you why you were there or how long you would be kept there?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. Nobody told us anything. We entered the stadium and then we waited to see what would happen next.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How long were you held at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: 46 days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can you just describe your -- if you can, your daily routine there. Tell me -- well, first of all, who guarded you at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: We were guarded by JNA soldiers. I didn't know any of them except for two. They changed every week. The shifts took place on Wednesdays.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And where did you sleep at night in this football stadium? I mean you personally.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I slept under the stands for the spectators and in locker rooms in which previously players changed and had showers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How many men were kept in this stadium? In other words, other than you and the other 700-odd men who arrived on the train, was there anybody else there already being held in the stadium?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. When we came, the stadium was empty.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And were you given any blankets or anything else to make those places you slept more comfortable?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. We didn't get anything. The first day, however, when we entered the stadium, we got a quarter of a loaf of bread and one pack of liver paste destined for four men to share.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Over the whole time you were at the stadium for that month and a half, was that the way -- was that typical of the food you were given? Can you describe whether the food provided was adequate?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. It was only the first day that we got that quarter of a loaf of bread and one pack of liver paste for four men. And the following days, we didn't get much food. We got some sort of tea, watery tea at that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you lose any weight while you were held there?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. In those 46 days I lost 11 kilos.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Tell me about drinking water and water for bathing. Was there adequate supply of water for those purposes?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. There was not enough water. Water was rationed. We had it between 9.00 and 11.00 in the morning, and in the afternoon from 1.00 to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell me what kind of medical care prisoners held in this stadium received.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: There was no medical care at all. Nobody lent us any medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And were there any deaths of prisoners while you were there, that you're aware of, during that month and a half?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. One man died, but he died from a serious disease, asthma.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How were you and the other prisoners treated while you were in that stadium? By the guards, I mean.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: We were treated very roughly. There was a roller we had to drag across the stadium to pluck grass out with our bare hands. We were treated very, very roughly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were you personally beaten at all while you were at the stadium? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Is that what you mean by "roughly"? I don't know exactly what you mean by that.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I personally wasn't beaten but I had to drag this roller for smoothening the path around the stadium.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there any other mistreatment, verbal mistreatment? Anything that scared you while you were there?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Profanities were common, the usual ones, the guards were telling us we were balijas, that we would be going to the front line to form the live shield, towards Bihac. That was the sort of intimidation we were subjected to.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Was there ever any -- were there ever any threats or attempts from people outside the stadium to get in and attack the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. The troops attempted that, the troops that passed along that road from Krupa towards Bosanski Novi, but the guards prevented that. Whenever such attempts were made, they made us find cover under the stands. I don't know what was the reason why they were protecting us in this way. Maybe they didn't want us to see what kind of equipment was being hauled across -- along the road, tanks or anything else. We couldn't -- we were not able to see.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: During this whole time that you were held there, were you able to change your clothes, get new clothes, or wash, do your -- launder your clothes?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: No. We were not able to do that. What I had on the first day I had on the last day when we reached Karlovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Were there any men being held there with you who, in your knowledge, were not ordinary civilians, who were -- had been engaged in any kind of armed combat at the time they were taken -- before they were taken there?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I didn't understand the question. What kind of armed combat do you mean? The people who were held at the stadium had not been involved in any sort of armed combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me, did you or any of the men there, try to get help from the outside? In other words, did you try to let the outside world in any way know that you were being held there, to seek some assistance?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. We tried. We had noticed vehicles belonging to the UNPROFOR moving from the direction of Croatia. Each day there were two such vehicles passing by. On these occasions we would stand up on the stands, and we would write "SOS" on leather jackets and on windows.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know whether this was ever seen? Did you get any signal that your calls for help had been understood?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. The UNPROFOR soldiers had noticed this. They turned their car on the road and flashed their lights at us. However, the guards got wind of it and they forbade us from using this part of the stadium where these stands were, facing the road.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you recognise -- I should have asked you this earlier: Did you know, personally know, any of the guards at the stadium?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Yes. I said at the beginning, I made acquaintance with two soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: That's right. Could you tell me their names, please.

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: That was this gentleman, Dragan Balaban from Josava, from the SDS, and another one, Momcilo Kenjalo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Dragan or Ranko?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: I got the name wrong again. I apologise. Ranko Balaban.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, he had the same name as the President of the SDS from Josava? It's two persons from Josava, both called Ranko Balaban, one of whom is the President of the SDS? Or are we talking of the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No -- in fact, yes, it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's get this right, because this is what we needed today. So Ranko Balaban, who was a guard in the stadium in Bosanski Novi, together with Momcilo Kenjalo, is the same Ranko Balaban to whom you have been referring to, whom you have mentioned earlier on today, as having met and negotiated with Sifet Barjaktarevic? Or isn't he the same one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. It's the same man.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that same man then became a guard in the stadium? From being the President of the SDS, holing negotiations with the President of the SDA, he becomes a guard in the stadium? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You got this right. Sifet, whenever he came back from a meeting of that sort, he said he had been together with him, that they had talks together, but to no avail.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And that was the village of Josava where Ranko Balaban was head of the crisis -- head of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: Witness BT82
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I'm not going to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No one is going to blame you for it, Mr. Nicholls, you're doing your duty here, and if you require more time, you will get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I wonder if we should break now. I'll be very quick Monday, just to finish up, and then I have this one administrative matter that I need to be in private session for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you anticipate finishing your cross-examination on Monday, Mr. Trbojevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. TRBOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. I need about an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We can draw down the curtains and the witness can leave. Sir, that's all for today. We will continue on Monday. We haven't finished with you as yet. So you will need to spend the weekend here. But on Monday, we will certainly finish with your testimony and you should be able to go back home. I thank you for having been patient.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you too. I apologise for all the mistakes I made with names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem. You're not the only one. Yes. I think, usher, you can escort him out of the courtroom and we will deal with these one or two administrative matters very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, you can start Mr. Nicholls, go ahead. Let's go into open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, this needs to be private for this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
